title: The Offering Document Is a Promise You Can Be Sued On
summary: An offering document is not a brochure. It is the record of what investors were told, and the law can hold the issuer and its people liable for what it says and what it leaves out. This lesson covers what the document must do, the concept of a material fact, and the sponsor's duty to the investors it manages.
body:
The offering document is the evidence of what you told your investors. Every statement in it, and every important fact left out of it, can be the basis of a claim. Write it as if it will be read aloud in a courtroom, because one day it might be.

Recall

Q. What is general solicitation?

A. Advertising or broadly publicising an offering to people the issuer has no existing relationship with. Many exemptions forbid or restrict it.

Q. What should a capital call clause always contain?

A. Who may call, for what purposes, up to what cap, with what notice, and the remedy if a partner does not pay, usually after a cure period.

Q. What is a correspondent banking relationship, in general terms?

A. An arrangement in which one bank provides services, such as payments in a foreign currency, to another bank. When correspondent relationships are cut, moving money across borders can become slow or impossible.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, last week was about whether you may raise money at all. This week is about what you owe the people who give it to you. That has two parts. Before they invest, you owe them a truthful and complete picture, set out in the offering document. After they invest, you owe them loyalty, care and honest reporting for as long as you manage their money. Nadia joins me later in the week because the second part is mostly accounting. Both parts are where sponsors who meant well get sued.

What the offering document does

In plain English: the offering document explains the deal so that an investor can decide whether to take the risk, and it records exactly what he was told.

Depending on the exemption and jurisdiction, the document may be prescribed, with required contents, or voluntary. Private placement documents are commonly called an offering memorandum or a private placement memorandum. Conceptually, a sound one covers the business and the project, the sponsor and its track record, the use of proceeds, the capital structure and the debt, the waterfall and every fee the sponsor or its affiliates will earn, conflicts of interest, the risk factors, financial information, investor rights, transfer and resale restrictions, and how investors will be reported to. Whether a particular document is required, and its exact contents, depends on the rules; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Material facts and misrepresentation

A material fact is one that a reasonable investor would consider important in deciding whether to invest, or one that would reasonably be expected to affect the value of the investment. Tests vary by regime, but the idea is the same everywhere. A misrepresentation is an untrue statement of a material fact, or an omission of a material fact needed to make what was said not misleading.

The second half of that definition catches most sponsors. You can be sued without telling a lie, by leaving out the fact that changes the meaning of the facts you did tell.

Worked example one, hypothetical. The document says, truthfully, "The construction contract is a fixed-price contract for 12,000,000 dollars." It does not say that the contract excludes foundation work, which is carried as a separate allowance of 800,000 dollars that the geotechnical report suggests is too low. Every word is true. The picture is misleading, because a reasonable investor reading "fixed price" would assume the main cost risk was capped. That omission is the kind of fact that can turn a true document into a misrepresentation.

Say that out loud now.

I can mislead without lying, by leaving out the fact that changes the meaning of what I said.

Forward-looking statements

Pro formas are projections, and projections will be wrong. The law in many jurisdictions treats forecasts differently from statements of present fact, but only if they are made honestly, with a reasonable basis, clearly identified as projections, and accompanied by the material assumptions and the factors that could make them wrong. A projected return with no stated assumptions, presented as near-certain, is the opposite.

Worked example two, hypothetical. Version A says: "Investors will receive an 18 percent IRR." Version B says: "Our base case projects an IRR of about 18 percent, assuming rents of 2.50 dollars per square foot per month, completion in 22 months and an exit capitalisation rate of 6 percent. A 6-month delay and an exit rate of 7 percent would reduce the projected IRR to about 9 percent. Investors could lose all of their investment." Version B gives a reasonable investor what he needs. Version A gives a lawyer what he needs.

The duty after they invest

Where you, as general partner or manager, control investors' money and the decisions about it, the law commonly treats you as owing fiduciary duties: a duty of loyalty, to put investors' interests ahead of your own in matters within the relationship and not to profit secretly from it, and a duty of care, to act with the skill and diligence the role requires. How far these duties apply, and how far an agreement can narrow them, depends on the vehicle and the law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. The practical consequence is clear: related-party contracts, fees to your own companies and opportunities you take for yourself must be disclosed and, where the agreement requires, approved.

How the best do it

Experienced sponsors put the offering document through a verification process before it is used: each factual statement is tied to a source document, such as the contract, the appraisal or the loan term sheet, and a named person signs off each section. A small developer can copy that directly: a verification table, one row per statement, with the source and the reviewer.

Omar's Six-Lens Check

Tax. The document should describe the investors' tax treatment only in general terms and tell them to take their own advice; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability. Liability for misrepresentation can reach the issuer and the individuals who sign or approve the document. Banking. The loan terms described must match the loan actually signed. Governance. Conflicts and related-party approvals must follow the agreement. Estate. Transfer rules on death must be disclosed. Exit. The exit described must reflect real resale restrictions and real refinance risk.

Updating the document

An offering document speaks as of its date. If something material changes before an investor subscribes, such as a new loan term, a revised cost or a delay, the document is out of date, and using it unchanged can itself be a misrepresentation. The usual practice is an amendment or supplement, delivered to everyone still considering the offering, and sometimes a right for those who have already subscribed to withdraw. Keep a dated version list, and never let anyone subscribe on a version you know is stale.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a document that is true sentence by sentence and misleading as a whole. The control is a verification table and a final read by someone outside the deal, asking one question: what would an investor want to know that this does not say?

The beginner's mistake

The beginner writes the offering document as a sales piece and lets the lawyer add risk factors at the end. The risks are part of the description of the deal, not a disclaimer after it.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the one-page memo: bottom line first, then the supporting facts, then the risks you would rather not mention. An offering document is that memo with legal liability attached. The habit of putting the uncomfortable fact on the first page is what protects you.

Recap

The offering document records what investors were told. A misrepresentation can be an untrue statement or a material omission. Projections need a reasonable basis, stated assumptions and real risks. After investment, a sponsor who manages the money commonly owes loyalty and care. Professional sign-off required: securities lawyer and, for financial information, a licensed accountant.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: Madoff, and what happens when the same hands hold the money and write the reports.
checklist: Does the document cover project, sponsor, use of proceeds, debt, waterfall, fees, conflicts, risks and reporting?
Is every factual statement tied to a source document in a verification table?
Have I asked what material fact a reasonable investor would want that is missing?
Is every projection labelled, with stated assumptions and a downside case?
Does the document say plainly that investors could lose everything?
Are all related-party fees and contracts disclosed?
Have securities counsel and an accountant reviewed it?
head: Field checklist
speak: The offering document records what my investors were told, and it can be sued on. It should explain the project, the sponsor, use of proceeds, the debt, the waterfall and every fee, conflicts, risks, financial information, rights, resale limits and reporting. A material fact is one a reasonable investor would consider important. A misrepresentation is an untrue statement of a material fact, or an omission that makes what I said misleading, so a document can be true sentence by sentence and still mislead, like calling a contract fixed price without saying the foundations are excluded. Projections need a reasonable basis, stated assumptions and a downside case. After they invest, as manager I commonly owe loyalty and care, so related-party dealings must be disclosed and approved. I verify every statement against a source and have someone outside the deal ask what is missing.
terms: Material fact — a fact a reasonable investor would consider important in deciding whether to invest, or that would reasonably affect the investment's value.
Misrepresentation — an untrue statement of a material fact, or an omission of a material fact needed to make a statement not misleading.
Fiduciary duty — a duty of loyalty and care owed by a person who controls another's money or interests within a relationship of trust.

hostile.q: Your document says the construction contract is fixed price. Is there any cost risk that isn't fixed?
hostile.a: Yes, and it is set out on the same page. The foundations are excluded and carried as an 800,000 dollar allowance, and the geotechnical report suggests that may be too low, so we show a downside case with a 400,000 dollar overrun funded from contingency. The verification table ties each statement to the contract and the report. If you think anything material is still missing, tell me and we will add it before anyone subscribes.

title: Madoff: When the Manager Writes His Own Reports
summary: Bernard Madoff's investment fraud, exposed in December 2008, was the largest of its kind and depended on one structural weakness: the same firm held the money, executed the trades and produced the statements investors relied on. This lesson takes it through seven steps and draws a rule for any developer who manages other people's money. Cole assists.
body:
For decades, Bernard Madoff's investors received statements showing steady gains on trades that did not happen. The fraud worked because no independent party stood between the money and the reports. That weakness is not unique to hedge funds. It exists in any small sponsor that holds investors' cash and writes their statements.

Recall

Q. What is a material omission?

A. Leaving out a fact a reasonable investor would consider important, where the omission makes what was said misleading.

Q. Why can a failed exemption behave like a contingent liability?

A. Because investors may have a right of rescission, called when the project is weakest.

Q. What is a capital control?

A. A government measure that restricts moving money into or out of a country.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this is the reference case for investor reporting and custody. Madoff did not build buildings, but the mechanism of his fraud applies directly to a real estate sponsor: whoever controls the bank account and produces the investor statements controls what investors believe. The facts below are those widely reported in the criminal case and the regulator's own internal review. Where I describe structure rather than specific figures, it is because the lesson is the structure.

1. Timeline

Madoff founded his firm in 1960 and became a prominent figure in the securities industry, including as a market maker. Alongside his brokerage business he ran an investment advisory operation for private clients and for feeder funds, which were funds that placed their own investors' money with him. From at least the early 1990s, and on his own later account possibly earlier, the advisory business was a Ponzi scheme: new investors' money paid existing investors' withdrawals, while statements reported trades that were not made. A financial analyst, Harry Markopolos, submitted detailed concerns to the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) from 2000 onwards. In late 2008, during the financial crisis, withdrawal requests surged. On 11 December 2008 Madoff was arrested after admitting the fraud to his sons, who reported him. He pleaded guilty in March 2009 and was sentenced in June 2009 to 150 years in prison. An SEC Inspector General report in 2009 found that the agency had received credible warnings over many years and failed to uncover the fraud.

2. Key decisions

For investors and feeder funds, the key decision was accepting an arrangement in which Madoff's own firm acted as investment manager, broker and custodian, holding the assets and producing the trade confirmations and statements. For the regulator, it was examining the firm without independently verifying, with third parties, that the trades and assets existed.

3. Assumptions

Investors assumed that a man so prominent in the industry, and so selective about whom he accepted, could not be running a fraud. Feeder funds assumed that because they had earned steady returns for years, the returns were real. Many assumed that a regulator had checked. Each assumption replaced verification with reputation.

4. Incentives

Feeder funds earned fees on the money they placed and had reasons not to ask questions that might end a profitable relationship. Investors enjoyed steady returns and had little reason to probe them. Madoff's incentive, once the fraud began, was to keep new money flowing to meet withdrawals. Nobody with access to the truth had an incentive to tell it.

Say that out loud now.

Reputation is not verification.

5. Warning signs ignored

Cole lists the signs that were raised publicly or in complaints over the years. Returns were unusually smooth, with very few losing months, which the strategy described could not plausibly produce. The firm held its own clients' assets, so there was no independent custodian. Trade confirmations were paper, produced by the firm. The firm's auditor was a very small accounting practice, out of all proportion to the size of the operation. And the strategy's volume of options trading, if real, should have been visible in the markets, and analysts could not find it.

6. Point of no return

For the scheme, the point of no return came in the 2008 crisis, when withdrawals exceeded new money and the payments could no longer be met. For investors, the last real chance to protect themselves was any moment before then when they could have demanded independent confirmation of the assets, or withdrawn.

7. Root cause

The root cause was structural: the same party controlled the money, the records of what was done with it, and the reports to investors, with no independent custodian, administrator or adequate auditor in between. Fraud needs an opportunity, and that structure supplied one for decades.

Cole's reading for a developer

A small real estate sponsor can recreate that structure without meaning to. You hold the project bank account, your company keeps the books, you prepare the investor statements, and your accountant is a friend who reviews them lightly. Even with complete honesty, investors then have no way to tell an honest sponsor from a dishonest one. Cole's controls: project funds in a bank account in the project entity's name, with dual signatories for large payments; statements prepared or reconciled by an independent administrator or accountant; an audit or review by a firm with the scale and independence to do it; bank confirmations sent directly to the auditor; and a right for investors to see the bank statements behind the report.

Why scale and independence matter

Ford draws one more lesson from the case. Controls only work if the people operating them are independent of the manager and big enough to do the job. A tiny auditor reviewing an enormous operation, or a friend reviewing a friend's statements, provides the appearance of a check without its substance. The questions an investor should ask of any sponsor, including you, are simple. Who holds the cash? Who reconciles the statements to the bank? Who audits them, and could that firm realistically check this volume of activity? Does the bank confirm balances to the auditor directly, or does the sponsor forward a copy?

Notice also what the regulator's failure teaches. An investor who assumes a regulator has verified everything is relying on a check that may not have been made, or may have been made badly. Regulation sets a floor. It is not a substitute for the controls an investor should require for himself.

Finally, the case shows how fraud grows. Once the first false statement is sent, every later statement must be false too, or the first is exposed. The safest point to stop a misreport is before the first one goes out, which is why independent reconciliation must exist from the first quarter, not be added when the fund is large.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk, for any sponsor, is a reporting structure in which investors cannot independently confirm that their money exists and is where the reports say. The control is separation: independent custody, independent preparation or reconciliation, and an auditor sized to the job.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks controls are only for people who might cheat. They are for honest people too, because they are the only way an honest sponsor can prove it.

Callback

In Week 61, Cole taught transfer pricing and the discipline of documenting related-party dealings at arm's length. Madoff is the extreme case of the same principle: when one party sits on both sides of every transaction, only independent evidence can show what really happened.

Recap

Madoff held the money, recorded the trades and wrote the reports, with no independent party in between, and warnings were ignored for years. The fraud ended when withdrawals overwhelmed new money in 2008. The prevention is structural separation between custody, records and reporting.

Rule 71: Never let investor reports come only from the hands that hold the money; keep project funds in the project's own account, have reports reconciled independently, and use an auditor with the scale and independence to check them.

Next: Nadia on The Money: what good investor reporting costs and what it is worth.
checklist: Are project funds held in an account in the project entity's name?
Do large payments need two signatories?
Is someone independent preparing or reconciling investor statements?
Is the auditor or reviewer sized to the job and independent of me?
Are bank confirmations sent directly to the auditor?
Can investors see the bank statements behind the reports?
Am I relying on anyone's reputation in place of verification?
head: Field checklist
speak: Bernard Madoff ran an investment advisory business that was a Ponzi scheme: new money paid withdrawals while statements reported trades that never happened. His firm was manager, broker and custodian, so it held the money and wrote the reports. Warnings, including detailed submissions by Harry Markopolos to the SEC from 2000, were not acted on, and the SEC's own Inspector General later found the agency failed to uncover it. In late 2008 withdrawals overwhelmed new money, and he was arrested on 11 December 2008, pleaded guilty in March 2009 and was sentenced in June 2009 to 150 years. The warning signs were smooth returns, self-custody, paper confirmations and a tiny auditor. The root cause was structural: no independent party between the money and the reports. Rule 71: keep funds in the project's own account, have reports reconciled independently, and use an auditor sized to the job.
terms: Ponzi scheme — a fraud in which returns to existing investors are paid from new investors' money rather than real profits.
Custodian — an independent institution that holds investors' assets, so the manager cannot move them without trace.
Feeder fund — a fund that pools its own investors' money and places it with another manager.

hostile.q: You keep the books, run the bank account and write our statements. How would I know if the numbers were wrong?
hostile.a: You should not have to trust me, so we have built the structure so you do not. Funds sit in the project entity's own account, with two signatories for large payments. An independent accountant reconciles each quarterly statement to the bank statements, which you may see on request. The annual audit is by a firm independent of me, and the bank confirms balances directly to the auditor.

rule: Rule 71: Never let investor reports come only from the hands that hold the money; keep project funds in the project's own account, have reports reconciled independently, and use an auditor with the scale and independence to check them.

title: What Good Investor Reporting Costs and What It Is Worth
summary: Investor reporting is a cost on every project and an asset on every raise that follows. This lesson prices a reporting and audit package, shows how it changes what the next investor will accept, and costs a restatement. Warrick's Wealth Ledger closes it.
body:
Good reporting is cheap insurance on your reputation and an investment in your next raise. Bad reporting is free until the day it costs you a project.

Recall

Q. What is a custodian?

A. An independent institution that holds investors' assets, so the manager cannot move them without trace.

Q. In a partner agreement, why should every remedy be modelled in dollars?

A. Because ownership percentages only matter through the money they produce at exit, and small percentage changes can be large sums.

Q. What is a source-of-funds check?

A. A bank's or professional's inquiry into where a customer's money came from, required under anti-money-laundering rules.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, reporting feels like overhead because it produces no square foot of building. But every investor you report to is either a future investor or a future complaint. The quality of your reports decides which. Today we put numbers on both sides, all hypothetical round figures.

What a reporting package contains

In plain English: investors need to know what happened to their money, what the project is worth, what has changed since the last report and what you expect next.

A sound quarterly package commonly contains a short letter with the bottom line first; budget against actual by major line; the schedule against baseline; a capital account statement for each investor, showing contributions, distributions, accrued preferred return and closing balance; material events, including changes to the loan, the contractor or the plan; related-party payments made in the period; and an updated forecast with the assumptions changed. Annually, financial statements, reviewed or audited by an independent accountant as the agreement requires.

Pricing the package

Worked example one, hypothetical. A 20,000,000 dollar project with 5,000,000 dollars of investor equity from 15 investors, over a four-year hold. An independent accountant to reconcile the quarterly package to the bank: 3,000 dollars a quarter, or 12,000 dollars a year. An annual audit by a firm of suitable scale: 25,000 dollars. Software and the sponsor's own time, valued at 10,000 dollars a year. Total about 47,000 dollars a year, or 188,000 dollars over four years.

Against a 20,000,000 dollar cost, 188,000 dollars is 0.94 percent. Against investor equity of 5,000,000 dollars, it is 3.8 percent over the hold, which is about 0.9 percent of equity a year. That is a real cost, and investors should see it disclosed as a project expense.

Say that out loud now.

Reporting costs under one percent of equity a year; it protects every raise after this one.

What it is worth

Now the other side. Suppose your second project needs 8,000,000 dollars of equity. Investors who received clear, verified, timely reports on the first are more likely to reinvest and to accept terms closer to what you propose. Assume, hypothetically, that a clean track record lets you set the preferred return at 8 percent rather than the 9 percent investors would otherwise demand from an unproven sponsor. On 8,000,000 dollars, one point is 80,000 dollars a year of priority return you do not have to pay before the promote begins. Over a four-year hold, that is roughly 320,000 dollars, before compounding effects in the waterfall. The reporting cost on project one was 188,000 dollars. The payback is plausible on the very next raise, and the benefit continues on every raise after it. These figures are illustrative; how investors price a track record is commercial practice and varies.

The cost of a restatement

Worked example two, hypothetical. A sponsor reports quarterly without reconciliation. In year two, the audit finds that 600,000 dollars of costs were capitalised incorrectly and that a related-party management fee of 150,000 dollars was never disclosed. The sponsor must restate two years of reports. Direct costs: additional audit work of 30,000 dollars and legal advice of 40,000 dollars. Indirect costs: three investors ask to be bought out, a lender asks for an explanation, and the next raise is delayed six months. If the delay costs 1 percent of a 10,000,000 dollar land price in extension fees, that is another 100,000 dollars. A restatement can easily cost more than the whole four-year reporting budget, and its reputational cost is not in the number.

The link to value

Reporting also affects the asset's value at exit. A buyer's due diligence relies on the rent roll, operating statements and capital expenditure records. Clean, audited records reduce the buyer's risk and the discount it applies for uncertainty. Disorganised records invite a price chip or a longer diligence period.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

For your personal balance sheet, your track record is an asset that does not appear on any statement. It lowers your cost of capital, which raises your share of every future deal's profit. Protect it as you would protect cash: report honestly, report early on bad news, and keep the evidence. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

Timeliness is part of quality

A report that arrives three months after the quarter ends is a history lesson, not a control. Investors cannot act on old information, and a sponsor who reports late invites the suspicion that something is being hidden. Set a deadline in the partnership agreement, for example 45 days after quarter end for the quarterly package and 120 days after year end for audited statements, though these are commercial choices, not standards. Then meet it, every time, and if you cannot, say why before the deadline passes.

Speed has a cost, because the accountant must work to a timetable, and it has a benefit, because it brings problems to the surface while they are still small. A late report on a troubled project is how a manageable overrun becomes a loss of trust.

Proportion: what a small sponsor can afford

None of this requires an institutional back office. A small developer can deliver most of the package with a disciplined spreadsheet, a template letter and an outside bookkeeper, and buy the independence where it matters most: the reconciliation to the bank and the annual audit or review. If the budget is tight, cut the formatting, not the independence. A plain report that is reconciled is worth more than a polished one that is not.

And keep the reporting consistent from quarter to quarter. Changing what you show, or how you calculate it, without saying so, is itself a warning sign to an experienced investor, because it is how bad numbers are usually hidden.

What disciplined sponsors do

Well-run sponsors publish the reporting calendar to investors at closing and treat it as a covenant to themselves. A small developer can copy that on the first deal: put the dates in the agreement, put them in a diary, and send a short note in advance whenever one will be missed, with the new date and the reason.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is cutting reporting cost to the bone and discovering, at audit or in a dispute, that the reports were wrong. The control is to budget independent reconciliation and audit from day one and disclose that cost in the offering document.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner measures reporting cost against the project. Measure it against your next raise and the price of a restatement.

Callback

In Week 12, Nadia taught owner accounting: accruals, capitalised costs and work in progress. The restatement in today's example is exactly that lesson going wrong: costs capitalised that should have been expensed. Investor reports are only as good as the accounting under them.

Recap

A reporting package covers budget, schedule, capital accounts, material events, related-party payments and forecasts, with independent reconciliation and an annual audit. Hypothetically it costs under one percent of equity a year. A clean record can repay that on the next raise, and a restatement can cost far more.

Next: LEX on The Rules: misrepresentation and fiduciary duty, and how liability attaches, with Canada and Guyana compared.
checklist: Does my quarterly package lead with the bottom line?
Does it show budget against actual and schedule against baseline?
Does each investor receive a capital account statement?
Are related-party payments listed every period?
Is the package reconciled to the bank by someone independent?
Is the reporting and audit cost budgeted and disclosed?
Have I priced what a restatement would cost me?
head: Field checklist
speak: Investor reporting is insurance on my reputation and an investment in my next raise. A sound quarterly package leads with the bottom line, then budget against actual, schedule against baseline, a capital account statement for each investor, material events, related-party payments and an updated forecast, reconciled to the bank by an independent accountant, with an annual audit. Hypothetically, on 5,000,000 dollars of equity, that costs about 47,000 dollars a year, under one percent of equity. On the other side, if a clean record lets me set an 8 percent preferred return instead of 9 percent on an 8,000,000 dollar second raise, that is about 80,000 dollars a year. A restatement, by contrast, costs audit and legal fees, buyout requests, lender questions and a delayed raise, often more than the whole reporting budget. My track record is an asset I protect like cash.
terms: Capital account statement — a report for each investor showing contributions, distributions, accrued preferred return and closing balance.
Restatement — the correction of previously issued financial reports found to be wrong.
Reconciliation — checking that the figures in a report agree with an independent source, such as bank statements.

hostile.q: Your reporting and audit costs are almost one percent of equity a year. Why should investors pay for that?
hostile.a: Because it is the only way you can verify that your money is where the reports say. The cost is disclosed in the offering document as a project expense. It pays for an independent accountant to reconcile every quarterly report to the bank and an independent annual audit. If you would prefer a lighter review in a particular year, we can discuss it, but I will not drop independent reconciliation.

title: Misrepresentation and Fiduciary Duty: How Liability Attaches
summary: When an offering document is wrong, liability can arise under securities statutes and under the general law, and it can reach individuals as well as the issuer. This lesson explains statutory and common law claims, the due diligence defence, and the duties a manager owes investors, then compares Canada and Guyana conceptually.
body:
Liability for a misleading offering can come from two directions: securities statutes that give investors a direct right of action, and the general law of misrepresentation and fiduciary duty. Your defence is mostly built before the document is used.

Recall

Q. What does a capital account statement show?

A. Each investor's contributions, distributions, accrued preferred return and closing balance.

Q. What is a shotgun clause?

A. A buy-sell clause where one partner names a price for the whole equity and the other must buy or sell at that price.

Q. What is foreign investment registration, conceptually?

A. A requirement in some countries to register incoming investment with an authority, which can affect the later right to repatriate profits and capital.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will sign offering documents, certificates and investor letters as a director or general partner. In many systems, that signature can make you personally answerable for what the document says. Knowing how liability attaches tells you what to do before you sign. This is conceptual teaching; liability rules, defences and limitation periods differ by jurisdiction, so verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Two routes to a claim

In plain English: an investor who was misled can sue under a special securities law, or under the ordinary law, and the special law is often easier for him.

A statutory right of action is a right to sue, created by a securities statute, for a misrepresentation in a prospectus or certain offering documents. Many such regimes give the investor a choice of rescission or damages, may treat the investor as having relied on the misrepresentation without proving it, and may extend liability beyond the issuer to defined persons, such as directors or those who signed. Some regimes require certain private offering documents to describe these rights. Under the general law, an investor can usually also sue for negligent or fraudulent misrepresentation, but must generally prove reliance and loss, which is harder.

Worked example one, hypothetical. An offering memorandum states that the project has "all approvals required to begin construction." In fact, a final building permit condition is unresolved and construction is delayed nine months. An investor who paid 200,000 dollars may, under a statutory regime of the kind described, seek rescission, returning his interest for his money, or damages for the loss in value. Under the general law he would need to show that he relied on that statement and that it caused his loss.

The due diligence defence

Many statutory regimes give individuals, and sometimes the issuer, a defence if they can show they conducted a reasonable investigation and had reasonable grounds to believe the statement was true, or did not know and could not reasonably have known it was false. The defence is about process. It is proved by evidence of the investigation made before the document was used.

Say that out loud now.

The due diligence defence is built before the document goes out, not after the complaint.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A director facing the approvals claim above can point to a verification table in which the approvals statement was tied to a letter from the municipality, reviewed by the planning consultant and approved by counsel, with the date. That record may support the defence. A director who simply read the draft and signed has nothing to show.

Fiduciary duty and its limits

Where a general partner or manager controls investors' money and decisions, it commonly owes a duty of loyalty: not to put itself in a position where its interest conflicts with the investors' without disclosure and consent, not to make secret profits, and not to take opportunities belonging to the venture. It also owes a duty of care. Limited partnership agreements often try to narrow these duties, for example by permitting the general partner's affiliates to earn fees or to pursue other projects. How far such narrowing is effective depends on the vehicle and the law. In general, courts are more willing to accept disclosed, specific permissions than broad exclusions, and are reluctant to permit a fiduciary to escape liability for bad faith.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is a conceptual comparison; verify against primary source before relying on any point. In Canada, securities regulation is provincial and territorial, coordinated through national instruments, and provincial statutes commonly provide statutory rights of action for misrepresentation in a prospectus and in certain offering memoranda, alongside the common law of misrepresentation; in Quebec the civil law also applies. In Guyana, securities activity is regulated under a securities statute administered by a securities regulator, with a legal system rooted in English common law, so common law claims for misrepresentation and breach of fiduciary duty are part of the background; the scope of any statutory right of action and how it is applied should be confirmed. [unverified — confirm independently] In both, the practical answer is the same: verify every statement, disclose every conflict, and keep the record.

Professional sign-off required: securities lawyer in each jurisdiction where investors live.

Who may be liable

Conceptually, the people who can face liability for a misleading offering include the issuer; its directors or the general partner's directors at the relevant time; those who signed the document; and sometimes promoters or experts whose reports are included, such as an appraiser or engineer, in relation to their own portion. Each regime defines the list differently, and some cap the damages certain individuals must pay; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. For you, the practical point is that becoming a director of your project vehicle is not a formality. It brings you onto the list.

Time limits

Claims are usually subject to limitation periods, which run from the purchase or from when the investor learned of the misrepresentation, and statutory rights of action often carry shorter periods than general law claims. You should not plan on a limitation period expiring; you should plan on the record being good enough that a claim fails. But know that the clock exists, and keep the offering file for at least as long as any claim could be brought, as advised by counsel.

Conflicts in practice

Most fiduciary disputes in real estate are not about theft. They are about conflicts: the sponsor's construction company, property manager or leasing agent earning fees from the project, a sponsor buying a neighbouring site for himself, or a sponsor's other project competing for the same tenants. The cure is the same each time: disclose specifically, in dollars or by formula; obtain approval where the agreement requires it, ideally from investors with no interest in the conflict; and keep the terms at market, with evidence such as competing quotes.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing an offering document without a record of how each statement was checked, which leaves you personally exposed with no due diligence defence. The control is a dated verification table, reviewed by counsel, kept with the offering file.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner relies on a broad disclaimer: "investors should not rely on this document." Disclaimers rarely defeat a statutory claim for a material misstatement, and a court may treat them as a sign the sponsor knew the document was unreliable.

Callback

In Week 21, LEX and Omar taught that limited liability protects shareholders but not the individual who personally commits a wrong. Securities statutes make that point directly: the director who signs a misleading document can be named personally, whatever the corporate structure.

Recap

Misled investors may sue under a statutory right of action, which can be easier, or under the general law. Individuals as well as the issuer can be liable. The due diligence defence depends on evidence of investigation made before the document was used. Managers owe loyalty and care, which agreements can only narrow so far.

Next: Nadia on The Numbers: building an investor's capital account statement, step by step.
checklist: Do I know which statutory rights of action apply in each investor's jurisdiction?
Is every statement in the document tied to a dated source in a verification table?
Has counsel reviewed the verification table before use?
Are all conflicts and affiliate fees disclosed specifically?
Do the agreement's limits on fiduciary duty rely on specific permissions rather than broad exclusions?
Am I relying on any disclaimer to cure a possible misstatement?
Is the offering file, with the verification record, retained securely?
head: Field checklist
speak: Liability for a misleading offering comes two ways. Securities statutes in many places give investors a statutory right of action for misrepresentation in a prospectus or certain offering documents, often with a choice of rescission or damages, sometimes without proving reliance, and reaching defined individuals such as directors or signers. The general law also allows claims for negligent or fraudulent misrepresentation, though reliance must usually be proved. The due diligence defence protects those who made a reasonable investigation and had reasonable grounds to believe the statement, so it must be built before the document goes out, in a dated verification table. Managers owe loyalty and care; agreements can narrow those duties with specific disclosed permissions, but rarely excuse bad faith. Canada's provincial regimes and Guyana's securities statute both sit on a common law base, but details must be confirmed locally.
terms: Statutory right of action — a right to sue created by a securities statute for misrepresentation in a prospectus or certain offering documents.
Due diligence defence — a defence available to those who conducted a reasonable investigation and had reasonable grounds to believe a statement was true.
Duty of loyalty — the fiduciary obligation not to profit secretly or act in conflict with those whose interests one manages.

hostile.q: The memorandum said all approvals were in place, and they were not. As a director, what is your defence?
hostile.a: My defence is the record we made before the memorandum was used. The verification table ties that statement to the municipality's letter, reviewed by our planning consultant and approved by counsel, with dates. If that letter was wrong, the table shows we investigated reasonably. Separately, I am not relying on a defence alone: we will disclose the issue to all investors now and offer those who want it a remedy.

title: Building an Investor's Capital Account Statement
summary: A step-by-step calculation, with hypothetical round numbers, of one investor's capital account over two years: contributions, accrued preferred return, distributions, return of capital and the equity multiple to date. The statement is the core of investor reporting, and every line must reconcile.
body:
An investor's capital account is the running answer to his first question: how much of my money is in, how much have I received back, and what am I still owed? Build it line by line, and make every line reconcile.

Recall

Q. What is the due diligence defence?

A. A defence, in many securities regimes, for those who made a reasonable investigation and had reasonable grounds to believe a statement was true.

Q. Why test a shotgun price from both sides?

A. Because the partner naming the price does not choose whether he buys or sells.

Q. What does know your client require of a bank?

A. Verifying a customer's identity, ownership and source of funds before and during the relationship.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most investor disputes begin with a number the investor does not understand or does not trust. A clear capital account statement prevents most of them. It also tests your own understanding of the waterfall: if you cannot produce this statement by hand, you do not yet understand what you promised. All figures below are hypothetical, and the terms, such as the preferred return rate and the order of payments, are commercial practice set by the partnership agreement, not standards.

Step 1: the terms

The investor commits 500,000 dollars to a limited partnership. The agreement gives investors an 8 percent per year preferred return, simple, not compounded, accruing on unreturned capital. Distributions are applied first to accrued preferred return, then to return of capital, then to the profit split. The investor funds in two instalments: 300,000 dollars on 1 January of year 1 and 200,000 dollars on 1 July of year 1.

Step 2: preferred return accrued in year 1

On the first 300,000 dollars, a full year at 8 percent: 300,000 times 0.08 equals 24,000 dollars. On the second 200,000 dollars, half a year at 8 percent: 200,000 times 0.08 times 0.5 equals 8,000 dollars. Total accrued in year 1: 32,000 dollars. No distributions are made in year 1, because the building is under construction.

Step 3: the year-end 1 statement

LineDollars
Capital contributed500,000
Capital returned0
Unreturned capital500,000
Preferred return accrued to date32,000
Preferred return paid to date0
Preferred return owed32,000

Say that out loud now.

Contributed, returned, unreturned; accrued, paid, owed. Every line reconciles to the one above it.

Step 4: year 2, with a distribution

The building completes and leases up. On 1 July of year 2, the partnership refinances and distributes; this investor's share is 120,000 dollars. First, accrue preferred return from 1 January to 1 July of year 2 on 500,000 dollars of unreturned capital: 500,000 times 0.08 times 0.5 equals 20,000 dollars. Preferred return owed is now 32,000 plus 20,000, which is 52,000 dollars.

Apply the 120,000 dollar distribution in the agreed order. First, 52,000 dollars clears the preferred return owed, leaving 68,000 dollars. Second, 68,000 dollars returns capital. Unreturned capital falls from 500,000 to 432,000 dollars. Nothing reaches the profit split.

Step 5: the rest of year 2

From 1 July to 31 December of year 2, preferred return accrues on the lower unreturned capital of 432,000 dollars: 432,000 times 0.08 times 0.5 equals 17,280 dollars. No further distributions are made.

Step 6: the year-end 2 statement

LineDollars
Capital contributed500,000
Capital returned68,000
Unreturned capital432,000
Preferred return accrued to date69,280
Preferred return paid to date52,000
Preferred return owed17,280
Total distributions to date120,000

Check the accrual: 32,000 plus 20,000 plus 17,280 equals 69,280 dollars. Check the payments: 52,000 dollars of preferred return plus 68,000 dollars of capital equals the 120,000 dollar distribution.

Step 7: the multiple to date

Equity multiple to date is total distributions divided by capital contributed: 120,000 divided by 500,000 equals 0.24 times. That figure must be shown with care. It is not a loss; most of the value is still in the building. So a fair report also shows the estimated value of the investor's remaining interest, labelled as an estimate with its basis, such as a recent appraisal or a stated capitalisation rate. If the investor's share of estimated net equity is 600,000 dollars, total value to paid-in capital is 120,000 plus 600,000, divided by 500,000, which is 1.44 times. The first number is cash. The second includes an estimate. Never blend them without saying so.

Step 8: what the investor should be able to check

Give the investor enough to check the statement himself. Show the dates and amounts of each contribution, the rate and basis of the preferred return, each accrual period with its capital base and days, and each distribution with its split between preferred return, capital and profit. With that, he can rebuild the numbers on a calculator, which is exactly the point. A statement an investor can recompute is a statement he is likely to trust.

Also reconcile the total of all investors' statements to the partnership. Add every investor's capital contributed, and it must equal the partnership's total contributed capital. Add every investor's share of the distribution, and it must equal the amount that left the partnership's bank account on that date. If the totals do not tie, one of the statements is wrong, and you must find it before any statement goes out.

Step 9: a common variation

Many agreements compound the preferred return annually rather than accruing it simply. Under annual compounding, any preferred return owed at the end of year 1 is itself added to the base for year 2. In this example, at the end of year 1 the 32,000 dollars owed would start earning 8 percent in year 2: an extra 32,000 times 0.08 times 0.5, which is 1,280 dollars, accruing by 1 July. The investor would then be owed 53,280 dollars at the distribution date rather than 52,000 dollars, and capital returned would fall by the same 1,280 dollars to 66,720 dollars. Small on one investor, material across a fund. Read the agreement's words exactly, and build the statement to them.

Step 10: the sponsor's side

The same arithmetic tells you, as sponsor, how far you are from the promote. Nothing reaches the profit split until all preferred return owed and all capital have been returned. At the end of year 2 this investor still has 432,000 dollars of capital and 17,280 dollars of preferred return ahead of you. Multiply across all investors and you have the hurdle your project must clear before you earn anything beyond your own share of capital and your fees. That number belongs in your own planning, every quarter, because it tells you how much of the next refinance or sale your investors will receive before any promote reaches you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a statement that applies distributions in the wrong order or blends cash with estimated value, so the investor cannot tell what he has actually received. The control is a statement built in the agreement's order, reconciled to the bank and the waterfall, with estimates labelled separately.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner keeps accruing preferred return on the original capital after some capital has been returned. Accrual follows unreturned capital, so it falls as capital comes back.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage taught levered and unlevered IRR, the equity multiple and their traps. The capital account is where those measures come from. An IRR quoted to an investor is only as good as the dated contributions and distributions in this statement.

Recap

Accrue preferred return on unreturned capital, by period. Apply each distribution in the agreed order: preferred return owed, then capital, then the split. Show contributed, returned, accrued, paid and owed, reconcile every line, and show cash multiples separately from estimated value.

Next: JAX on The Room: the investor call when the numbers are late and bad.
checklist: Have I used the agreement's preferred return rate, basis and order of payments?
Is preferred return accrued by period on unreturned capital?
Is each distribution applied in the agreed order?
Do accrued, paid and owed preferred return reconcile?
Do capital contributed, returned and unreturned reconcile?
Is the cash multiple shown separately from any estimated value?
Is any estimated value labelled with its basis and date?
head: Field checklist
speak: Here is one investor's capital account, hypothetical. He commits 500,000 dollars at an 8 percent simple preferred return on unreturned capital: 300,000 on 1 January and 200,000 on 1 July of year 1. Year 1 accrual is 24,000 plus 8,000, so 32,000 dollars, with no distributions. On 1 July of year 2, another 20,000 accrues, so 52,000 is owed. A 120,000 dollar distribution pays the 52,000 first, then returns 68,000 of capital, leaving 432,000 unreturned. The second half of year 2 accrues 17,280 on that lower base. Year-end: contributed 500,000, returned 68,000, unreturned 432,000, accrued 69,280, paid 52,000, owed 17,280. The cash multiple is 0.24 times; including a labelled estimate of 600,000 dollars of remaining value, 1.44 times. I never blend cash and estimate without saying so.
terms: Unreturned capital — the capital an investor has contributed less the capital returned to him.
Equity multiple to date — total cash distributions divided by capital contributed, measured at a date.
Total value to paid-in — distributions plus the estimated value of the remaining interest, divided by capital contributed.

hostile.q: Your statement shows a 1.44 multiple, but I have only received 120,000 dollars on 500,000. Isn't that misleading?
hostile.a: It would be if I showed only the 1.44. The statement shows the cash multiple first, 0.24 times, which is the 120,000 dollars you have received. Separately, labelled as an estimate, it shows 1.44 times including our estimate of your remaining interest, based on the appraisal dated in the footnote. You can rely on the first number; the second depends on that appraisal and the market.

title: The Investor Call When the Numbers Are Late and Bad
summary: A realistic scene: a cost overrun and a delay mean the next distribution will not be paid, and the quarterly report is late. This lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind investors' questions, when to stay silent and how to hold your state on a call where you carry the bad news.
body:
Bad news gets worse with age. Tell investors early, in the order that matters to them: what happened, what it means for their money, what you are doing about it, and when they will hear from you next.

Recall

Q. In a capital account, what does preferred return accrue on?

A. On unreturned capital, by period, so it falls as capital is returned.

Q. What should you say when a friend asks to invest before any raise is set up?

A. That you cannot discuss investing outside a proper legal process, without naming any return or saying the investment is safe.

Q. Why do banks sometimes close accounts without explanation?

A. Often because of risk or compliance concerns, such as unexplained flows or high-risk jurisdictions, and they may be restricted in what they can say.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every sponsor eventually makes this call. How you make it decides whether investors stay with you for the next deal and whether a disappointing project becomes a dispute. On Day 4, LEX showed that a misleading report can create liability; today is about telling the truth well. The scene and figures are hypothetical.

The scene

A 15-investor limited partnership. The contractor has reported a 900,000 dollar overrun on facade work, and completion moves from month 22 to month 28. The distribution investors were told to expect next quarter will not be paid. The quarterly report is two weeks late because the forecast had to be rebuilt. You have called a video meeting, with a written update sent an hour before.

The opening

Lead with the bottom line. "Thank you for joining. I'll give you the headline first. Completion has moved six months, to month 28, and there is a 900,000 dollar overrun on the facade. That means there will be no distribution next quarter. Your capital is not at immediate risk: the overrun is funded from contingency and a sponsor loan I am making, and the construction loan remains in balance. I'll take you through each part, then answer every question."

Say that out loud now.

Headline first: what happened, what it means for your money, what I am doing.

The question behind the question

Investors will ask "Why didn't we know sooner?" Behind that is "Can I trust your reports?" Answer both. "The contractor flagged a possible issue six weeks ago. I chose to confirm the number before reporting it, and that delayed the report. In hindsight I should have told you there was an issue under review. From now on, I'll report material issues as soon as they are known, with the uncertainty stated." That admission protects your credibility more than any defence would.

Others will ask "What's my return now?" Behind that is "Am I going to lose money?" Give the revised base case, with its assumptions, and the downside: "The revised base case projects about 12 percent rather than 16 percent, assuming the current rent forecast. If rents come in 5 percent lower as well, it is about 8 percent. Your full statements, with the assumptions, are in the update."

The lines to say

State facts with their sources: "The monitor's report of the 14th confirms the overrun figure." Separate what is known from what is estimated. Say what you are personally doing: "I am lending 300,000 dollars to the partnership on the terms in the agreement, repaid after your preferred return." Name the next contact: "You'll receive a written update on the facade claim in two weeks, whether or not it is resolved."

The lines never to say

Never say "Don't worry" or "It will all work out." Never blame a named subcontractor or consultant on the call; disputes may follow and your words can be used. Never give a new return figure without its assumptions. Never say "This is confidential, don't share it," to some investors and not others; information must reach all investors equally. And never say anything on the call that is not in the written update.

When to stay silent

Stay silent after the headline, to let investors absorb it. Stay silent when an investor expresses anger; let him finish, then acknowledge it. Stay silent rather than speculate on a question you cannot answer: "I don't know yet. I'll confirm in the written update on the 28th."

Holding your state

You will feel shame and the urge to over-explain. Both are normal and both make the call longer and less clear. Prepare a one-page script with the headline, three facts, your actions and the next date. Have a colleague take notes, so you can listen. Before the call, while seated, a few slow breaths with a longer exhale can steady your voice; check that with your doctor if you have any relevant condition.

Personal brand

This month's thread is personal brand. In this business, your brand is not your logo or your social media. It is what investors say about you after a bad quarter. A sponsor who reported early and honestly when things went wrong is the one investors call first for the next deal.

Ask yourself one question after every hard call: if the investors described today to someone who has never met me, what would they say? Make the next call so that the answer is the one you want.

After the call

Within a day, send every investor a short written note of what was said, including the questions asked and your answers, and correct anything you said on the call that was imprecise. Investors who could not attend must receive the same information as those who did. Log the call in your investor record with the date, attendees and the note. If an investor asks a question in private afterwards, answer it in writing, and if the answer is material, share it with all investors.

Then do what you said you would, on the dates you said. The investors' trust after a bad-news call is rebuilt not by the call itself but by the next three reports arriving on time and saying exactly what happened. A sponsor who promises an update on the 28th and sends it on the 27th has done more for his reputation than any explanation.

When an investor wants out

One investor may ask to sell his interest or demand his money back. Do not make a private promise on the call. Explain that transfers and redemptions follow the partnership agreement and securities resale rules, that you will look at the request with counsel, and that any arrangement offered to one investor will be considered fairly for all. Treating one investor better than the others, quietly, to end a complaint, is exactly the kind of conflict LEX warned about on Day 4. Equal treatment is not only good manners; it is part of the duty you owe, and it is what the other investors will judge you on when they hear about it, as they eventually will.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is delaying bad news until it is certain, so the first investors hear of it is a missed distribution. The control is a rule: report a material issue as soon as it is known, with its uncertainty stated, in writing to all investors at once.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner softens the headline and buries it in the third paragraph. Investors notice, and they stop believing the first paragraph of every future report.

Callback

In Week 5, Kema taught bottom line first and the pyramid principle. On a bad-news call those habits are not style; they are honesty. The order you speak in tells investors whether you are hiding something.

Recap

Send the written update first, open with the headline, separate facts from estimates, state what you are doing and when they will hear next. Answer the trust question behind each question, never speculate, never say anything not in writing, and treat every investor equally.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: Week 71's six questions, the Red Pen and the boardroom drill.
checklist: Did I send the written update before the call?
Did I open with the headline: what happened, what it means, what I am doing?
Did I separate known facts from estimates, with sources?
Did I give any revised return with assumptions and a downside?
Did I avoid blaming named parties on the call?
Did every investor receive the same information at the same time?
Did I name the date of the next update?
head: Field checklist
speak: When numbers are late and bad, I tell investors early, in writing first, then on a call that opens with the headline: completion has moved six months, there is a 900,000 dollar overrun, there will be no distribution next quarter, and here is how it is funded and why the loan stays in balance. When they ask why they didn't know sooner, the real question is whether they can trust my reports, so I admit I should have flagged the issue while confirming it, and commit to reporting material issues as soon as known. Any revised return comes with assumptions and a downside. I never say don't worry, never blame a named party, never share information with some investors and not others, never say anything not in the written update, and I always name the next date. My brand is what investors say about me after a bad quarter.
terms: Material issue — an event or change a reasonable investor would consider important to the value or timing of the investment.
Equal disclosure — giving the same material information to all investors at the same time.
Revised base case — an updated central forecast, with its changed assumptions stated.

hostile.q: You knew about the facade problem six weeks ago. Why should I believe your next report?
hostile.a: Because I am telling you plainly that I should have told you sooner. I waited to confirm the number, and that was the wrong call. From today, any material issue goes to all investors in writing as soon as it is known, with the uncertainty stated. You will have the independent monitor's report attached to every update, and the accountant's reconciliation, so you do not have to rely on my word.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 71 Review: Offering Documents, Liability and Reporting
summary: Six questions test the week's ideas: material facts and omissions, projections, statutory and general law claims, the due diligence defence, fiduciary duty and the capital account. The Red Pen marks up a hypothetical investor letter, and a two-minute boardroom drill closes the week.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: what you tell investors before they invest, and every report after, must be complete, verified and independent of the hands that hold the money, because it is what you will be judged on.

Recall

Q. What is general solicitation?

A. Broadly publicising an offering to people the issuer has no existing relationship with, which many exemptions restrict.

Q. What does a deadlock ladder end in?

A. A mechanism one partner can trigger alone, such as a buy-sell or forced sale, with an agreed valuation method.

Q. Why does foreign investment registration matter at exit?

A. Because in some countries the right to repatriate profits and capital depends on the investment having been registered when it came in.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the sponsors who last are not the ones with the best first deal. They are the ones whose investors trusted every word, in good quarters and bad. If you can answer these six questions aloud, you understand where that trust is legally anchored. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. How can an offering document mislead without containing a false statement?

Answer: By omitting a material fact needed to make what was said not misleading, such as describing a contract as fixed price without saying major work is excluded.

Question 2. What makes a projection defensible?

Answer: It is made honestly with a reasonable basis, clearly labelled as a projection, with its material assumptions and a downside case, and a plain statement that investors could lose their money.

Question 3. What is the difference between a statutory right of action and a general law claim?

Answer: A statutory right of action is created by a securities statute and is often easier for investors, sometimes without proving reliance, and can reach defined individuals; a general law claim usually requires proof of reliance and loss.

Question 4. How is the due diligence defence built?

Answer: Before the document is used, through a reasonable investigation recorded in a dated verification table tying each statement to a source, reviewed by counsel.

Question 5. What was the root cause in Madoff, and what is the developer's version of the control?

Answer: The same party held the money, recorded the trades and wrote the reports. The control is funds in the project's own account, independent reconciliation of reports and an auditor sized to the job.

Question 6. In a capital account, in what order is a distribution applied, and on what does preferred return accrue?

Answer: In the agreement's order, commonly preferred return owed, then return of capital, then the split; preferred return accrues on unreturned capital, by period.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

JAX explained the offering document, material facts and fiduciary duty. Ford and Cole took Madoff through seven steps, giving Rule 71. Nadia priced reporting against the cost of a restatement. LEX explained how liability attaches and compared Canada and Guyana. Nadia built a capital account statement. JAX ran the bad-news investor call.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical quarterly letter and find the defects before reading on.

Dear Investors, another strong quarter! Construction is progressing well and we remain confident in our projected 18 percent IRR. Our audited results show the project on budget. Minor items with the facade contractor are being resolved. As always, our affiliate continues to provide project management at standard rates. Distributions will resume shortly. Please keep this letter confidential. Warm regards, the General Partner.

The defects. First, "another strong quarter" with no figures: no budget against actual, no schedule against baseline, no capital account. Second, "projected 18 percent IRR" with no assumptions and no downside. Third, "audited results" for a quarterly letter is very likely false; quarterly figures are rarely audited, and calling them audited is a misstatement. Fourth, "minor items with the facade contractor" may conceal a material overrun or delay. Fifth, the affiliate's fee is mentioned but not quantified, and "standard rates" is not disclosure of a related-party payment. Sixth, "distributions will resume shortly" implies a pause that has not been explained and promises timing without basis. Seventh, "keep this letter confidential" is fine only if all investors receive the same letter; it must never be a way to treat investors differently. And eighth, there is no date for the next update and no independent reconciliation mentioned.

How the letter should read

In outline: open with the headline and the numbers, budget against actual by major line, the schedule against baseline, any change to completion or to distributions with the reason, the facade issue quantified with what is known and what is estimated, related-party payments listed in dollars, the revised forecast with assumptions and a downside, the capital account statements attached, the independent accountant's reconciliation noted, and the date of the next update.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a new investor who asks, "Why should I trust what you send me?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because you do not have to take my word for it. Before you invest, the offering document tells you everything a reasonable investor would want to know, including the risks and every fee my companies earn, and each statement in it was checked against a source document and reviewed by counsel. Projections are labelled, with assumptions and a downside. After you invest, your money sits in the project's own account, with two signatures for large payments. Every quarter you get budget against actual, the schedule, your own capital account and any related-party payments, reconciled to the bank by an independent accountant, and an independent audit every year. If something goes wrong, you hear it from me early, in writing, at the same time as every other investor. That is how I protect your money and my reputation."

Score yourself: bottom line first? Disclosure of fees and conflicts? Independent custody and reconciliation? Early bad news? Two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

A last drill on independence

Before closing the week, run one more check on your own future structure. Write down, for a hypothetical first project, the name of the bank where project funds will sit, who can sign, who will prepare the quarterly package, who will reconcile it to the bank, who will audit or review the annual statements, and how the bank's confirmation will reach that auditor. If any two of those roles are filled by the same person, or by you, mark it and decide what you will change. Rule 71 is easy to agree with in a lesson and easy to break on a small first deal, when doing everything yourself feels efficient. Efficiency is not the test. The test is whether an investor could check you without trusting you.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is reporting that is self-prepared, unreconciled and optimistic, so investors cannot tell a good sponsor from a bad one until it is too late. The control is Rule 71: separate custody, records and reports, and verify everything.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the investor letter as marketing. It is a record, and it may be read later by a regulator, a court or a buyer.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco taught the owner's charter, governance and the owner decision log. Investor reporting is the same discipline turned outward: decisions recorded at the time, approvals evidenced, and a single version of the truth sent to everyone who has a right to it.

Recap

Offering documents must be complete and verified; omissions can mislead. Projections need a basis, assumptions and a downside. Statutory and general law claims can reach individuals, and the due diligence defence is built before use. Managers owe loyalty and care. Capital accounts apply distributions in order and accrue on unreturned capital. Rule 71 separates the money from the reports.

Next: REGA, with Cole, on First Principles: integrity, anti-money-laundering checks, source of funds and beneficial ownership.
checklist: How can an offering document mislead without a false statement?
What makes a projection defensible?
What is the difference between a statutory right of action and a general law claim?
How is the due diligence defence built?
What was the root cause in Madoff, and what is the developer's control?
In a capital account, in what order is a distribution applied, and on what does preferred return accrue?
head: The six questions
speak: What I tell investors must be complete, verified and independent of the hands that hold the money. An offering document can mislead by omission, so I ask what a reasonable investor would want that is missing. Projections need a reasonable basis, labels, assumptions and a downside. Misled investors may have a statutory right of action, often easier than a general law claim and able to reach individuals who sign, so I build the due diligence defence before use, with a dated verification table reviewed by counsel. As manager I owe loyalty and care, so every related-party fee is disclosed in dollars. Madoff's root cause was that one party held the money and wrote the reports; Rule 71 keeps funds in the project's account, reports independently reconciled and an auditor sized to the job. Capital accounts apply distributions in order and accrue on unreturned capital, and bad news goes out early, to everyone at once.
terms: Verification table — a record tying each statement in an offering document to its source document, reviewer and date.
Related-party payment — a payment from the project to the sponsor or a company connected to it, which must be disclosed.
Independent reconciliation — an outside accountant's check that investor reports agree with bank and accounting records.

hostile.q: Your letter called the quarterly results audited. Were they?
hostile.a: No, and that word should not have been used. Quarterly figures are reconciled to the bank by an independent accountant; only the annual statements are audited. I will correct it in writing to all investors this week, state exactly what each level of review covers, and our template now requires the accountant to approve any description of their work before a letter goes out.
